data.title: SA analyst says Treasury yields are the market’s next big catalyst
data.description:
Wall Street pulled back Friday as investors digested stronger-than-expected jobs data, while market attention increasingly turned toward Treasury yields and their potential impact on equities and cryptocurrencies.

Seeking Alpha analyst Alex King of Cestrian Capital Research said the week’s trading showed resilience despite pressure on major indexes to break below key technical levels. 

“This week saw the major equity indices eke out modest gains after threatening to sell down below their key short-term moving averages,” King stated.

On Friday the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJI) declined -0.5%, while the S&P 500 (SP500) fell -0.3% and the Nasdaq Composite (COMP:IND) lost -0.2%. 

King noted that Bitcoin (BTC-USD) and Ether (ETH-USD) posted gains during the week, while companies holding cryptocurrencies in their treasuries significantly outperformed. Oil (CL1:COM) prices also edged higher, although futures and exchange-traded funds failed to establish a sustained upside breakout. 

“The real story is in yields,” King said, arguing that Treasury rates could become the next major catalyst for financial markets.

“We think yields are headed down, soon,” he stated, adding that falling yields could push equities to new highs while encouraging additional capital to enter the cryptocurrency market. 

King said such a move could ultimately attract “late money into this new bull market in crypto,” reinforcing his constructive outlook despite Friday’s market decline.

data.title: September Fed hike 'wouldn't be the worst thing' for stocks - Citi's Chronert
data.description:
Citi analyst Scott Chronert said Friday a preemptive Federal Reserve rate hike in September "wouldn't be the worst thing" for equity markets (SPY) (DIA) (QQQ). Given elevated concerns about the Fed's next move, Chronert believes markets would likely look through such an action and view it somewhat positively—though the critical question becomes whether investors are facing one or two hikes, or the start of an entirely new rate-hiking cycle.

While Citi is not overly concerned about a full-blown rate-hiking cycle materializing, Chronert emphasized that equity valuations critically depend on stability at the long end of the yield curve (TLT) (TLH) (ZROZ). "What I do need is a stable back end of the curve to support the valuation setup," he told CNBC in an interview, noting his team is focused squarely on where the 10-year Treasury yield (US10Y) is headed rather than obsessing over Fed funds alone.

Chronert is maintaining his 8,100 year-end S&P 500 (SP500) price target, which would require roughly one percent monthly gains through year-end. He expects Q3 earnings season to provide fundamental support for equities. Beyond that, navigating the midterm elections should give way to a relief rally opportunity that sets up a positive path into December. The AI (AIQ) (AIEQ) narrative, he added, continues to unfold more positively than not.

On mega-cap (MGC) growth and technology (XLK), Chronert acknowledged a mixed third quarter so far—tech in aggregate has been roughly a market performer, but that result masks a software (IGV) surge offset by a semiconductor (SMH) selloff. The mega-cap growth cohort, representing 35% to 50% of the index depending on measurement, has delivered uneven performance and influence on broader index action. 

Looking ahead, Chronert expects this group to find its footing as confidence builds around the persistence of the AI investment theme into 2027 and beyond, supporting continued market breadth. "That fundamental picture still net-net is pretty constructive," he said.

data.title: South Korea says Air Products, three other U.S. firms pledge $2B in chip, energy projects
data.description:
Four U.S. companies have pledged a combined $2B in direct investments in South Korea spanning semiconductors, advanced materials, and renewable energy, South Korea's Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said Friday.

Air Products (APD) will install gas supply facilities at its next-generation semiconductor production base at Pyeongtaek, aiming to enhance the domestic materials supply chain by equipping the facility with production capabilities for ultra-high purity gas, rare gases for micro-processes, and hydrogen, which are essential for semiconductor manufacturing.

Axcelis Technologies (ACLS) will expand production ‌of ⁠ion implantation systems at its operations in Pyeongtaek - the company's only ion implanter manufacturing base outside the U.S. - adding engineering, prototype development, and training capabilities, thus broadening the plant's role beyond production.

Corning (GLW) will upgrade its production facility in Asan by introducing next-generation process technology to strengthen its position in advanced ​glass and ​other materials ⁠used in displays and semiconductors.

Finally, Pacifico Energy will ​move forward with ⁠a 3.2 GW offshore wind project near Jindo in the country's southwest to support a new semiconductor manufacturing hub.

data.title: Higher feed costs present a new headwind for Cal-Maine Foods -- StoneX
data.description:
With feed costs rising, Cal-Maine (CALM) is expected to face another earnings headwind even as egg prices seem to be bottoming. This led StoneX analyst Ben Klieve to downgrade the stock to Hold from Buy and remove his $100 price target.

“We had been expecting an effectively flat feed input cost in FY27, now likely to be up more than 10%, a level that could be worse if not for the positive impact of Cal-Maine’s pivot towards cost-plus contracts,” Klieve writes in a note to clients.

Front-month corn prices have spiked 15% since mid-August, and since then conditions have only worsened with feed costs materially higher year-over-year, representing a “material headwind” especially for the low-margin commodity egg segment.

For patient investors, Klieve believes the cyclical trough in commodity egg markets coupled with Cal-Maine’s ramp to higher-margin specialty eggs and significant growth from its strategic pivot to prepared offerings “are all valuable catalysts.” However, Klieve’s downgrade to Hold reflects an increased expectation for “muted profitability” into FY28, “not a change in our favorable long-term sentiment.”

Cal-Maine (CALM) shares are down another 2% on Friday, bringing the three-day loss to 5.3% and putting the stock in the red for a second week.

data.title: TSLA false breakout: No Musk, no stream, no follow-through
data.description:
Tesla (TSLA) shares dropped -5.9% Friday and sit -21.2% lower for 2026 after Thursday’s breakout failed to hold. Traders now treat the move as a potential false breakout unless TSLA reclaims $370 on stronger momentum.

The reversal followed Tesla’s Cybercab launch in Austin, which offered no livestream, no Elon Musk appearance, and no financial details on robotaxi scaling. Barclays’ Dan Levy called the lack of communication disappointing and said the event may prove a weaker catalyst than expected without new growth targets. 

Shares had risen beforehand on hopes the two-seat autonomous vehicle would advance Tesla’s robotaxi plans against Waymo. Optimism faded after NHTSA opened a probe into the Cybercab’s self-certification under federal safety standards, citing the absence of a steering wheel and pedals. Possible state resistance to camera-only sensors added uncertainty. 

The rollout remains limited to a geofenced Austin zone. RBC’s Thomas Ito said volume concerns look overblown, calling the measured pace an intentional strategy rather than a technology limit. CFO Vaibhav Taneja had flagged avoiding early failures that could hinder expansion into Dallas and Houston. 

Investors remain unsure whether Tesla can scale the cautious launch into an autonomous network under NHTSA scrutiny.

data.title: U.S. Justice Dept. puts pause on cooperation with Canada on antitrust - WSJ
data.description:
The U.S. Department of Justice's antitrust division has been instructed to stop all work with the Canadian government. 

Lynda Marshall, the chief of the antitrust division's international section, ordered officials to stop all cooperation on cases and engagement on policy issues with Canadian authorities, according to a WSJ report on Friday, which cited a Wednesday email with the subject line "Pause on Canada,"  She provided no reason for the directive but said she would "circle back if the guidance changes."

The Justice Department and the White House didn't immediately respond to WSJ requests for comment. Representatives for the Canadian prime minister and the Competition Bureau didn't immediately respond.

The news comes as a trade war between Canada and the U.S. has been escalating in recent weeks. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government sees little chance of resuming talks  with President Donald Trump before the midterm elections after trade negotiations collapsed, Bloomberg reported last week.

data.title: U.K. government set to approve controversial North Sea gas field this month, reports say
data.description:
The U.K. government is expected to approve development of the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea later this month, according to the BBC and several other reports.

The Guardian also reported that Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is expected to approve the Rosebank oil field in the coming months.

Jackdaw and Rosebank are operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell (SHEL) and Equinor (EQNR), with Ithaca Energy (ITHLF) (ITHEY) also owning 20% of Rosebank.

Both projects were approved by the former Conservative government in 2022 but were struck down by a ruling from a Scottish court after a challenge from environmental groups arguing that consent was given without fully considering their climate impact.

Neither field is large, with Jackdaw and Rosebank forecast to have ​peak production of 40K boe/day and 70K boe/day, respectively.

Adura has said the Jackdaw field could produce 6% of the U.K.'s total gas output at its peak, although environmental groups believe it will meet just 2% of U.K. gas demand over its 10-year lifetime.

The JV has also said developing both fields would generate £1.4B (~$1.9B) in tax revenues by 2029.

data.title: Boston Scientific restoring shipping after cyberattack
data.description:
Boston Scientific (BSX) traded higher on Friday after the cardiac device maker said it has begun restoring shipping capabilities for most of its products across its major distribution centers worldwide after a recent cybersecurity incident.

Shares of the Marlborough, Massachusetts-based MedTech fell last week after the company disclosed that a cybersecurity incident had affected some of its IT systems and disrupted its worldwide operations.

With assistance from CrowdStrike (CRWD) and other outside experts, Boston Scientific (BSX) said that it is becoming increasingly confident that unauthorized access was restricted to only some of its internal-facing IT infrastructure.

“As capabilities are validated and brought back online, we are progressively moving customer orders through the fulfillment process,” the company said in a statement after the close, adding that it will take some time for it to clear the current backlog.

“We are working expeditiously to restore shipping capabilities for additional products and locations as validation is completed and will continue to work to ramp up to full capacity,” Boston Scientific (BSX) noted.

TD Cowen welcomed the update, with analyst Joshua Jennings viewing “yesterday’s news as a big step forward for the company, and I think that today’s stock reaction fails to reflect this progress.” Jennings has a Buy rating and a $56 target on the stock.

data.title: Trump administration working on post-war Middle East strategy - report
data.description:
The Trump administration has started crafting a sweeping post-war strategy for the Middle East, intended to reshape U.S. engagement in the region once the Iran conflict concludes, according to a media report on Friday.

The framework, still in early development, is taking shape across both senior political levels and multiple agencies, Axios reported, citing two U.S. officials and two other sources with knowledge of the matter.

Three main pillars have reportedly emerged: building a U.S.-guaranteed regional alignment among allies to contain Tehran; securing broader regional stability by advancing the next phase of President Trump's Gaza plan, reaching a security agreement between Israel and Syria, and implementing the Israel-Lebanon agreement; and expanding the Abraham Accords toward the ultimate goal of Saudi-Israeli normalization.

The planning unfolds against a tight political calendar, with Israel's Oct. 27 elections and U.S. midterms in November looming over deliberations.

Trump has held two meetings with senior advisers in recent weeks to discuss the plan and privately told associates he's working on "something much bigger" in the Middle East after the Iran war, which is now in its sixth month, sources told Axios.

Administration officials stressed Trump intends to push forward regardless of Israeli election results—even if they produce a political stalemate.
